Homeschooling: The Best Hope for Americas Future

I'm in a really good place right now with home schooling. We are in year two and I know we made the right decision. I wish that I'd known all the resources and groups that are out there to support homeschoolers. If any of you would like support or help getting started, I am at your service! I'd really like a conservative home schooling buddy, even if it's just online.

Care to share your resources? Looking for guidelines, books, plans, or timelines to help form a structure to which curriculum can be added. Obviously the curriculum is important as well, but the structure of such needs to come first.
I'm also interested in the resources that you use.

@51rH0n3y84d93r and @FishsticksForever:

I will provide a list of books and links that have worked for us at the end of this post, but I think the most important thing to remember is that flexibility is key. The most beautiful, expensive curriculum in the world is worthless if your kid hates it and there are tears and fighting when those books come out. You'll be miserable and no one can learn when they are upset. That being said, I'll only put down what we actually use and love.

The book that really convinced me I had the resources within myself to homeschool my child was Grace Llewellyn's Guerilla Learning. It's kind of been my bible. John Taylor Gatto's Dumbing Us Down gives me fire and energy because it pisses me off. John Holt, the father of homeschooling, wrote How Children Learn, which is a good place to start. I highly recommend taking a look at the Homeschool Legal Defense Association's website. If you live in a more rigid state, they will be a good investment in case you run into any pushback from local authorities. I believe they also provide information about what is required in order to homeschool within the law in each state. https://hslda.org/

You can get templates for logging hours and activities online. Some people make their own spreadsheets. I hand write this stuff in a day timer type calendar because I'm old fashioned that way. At the beginning of the week I write down my goals for that week. This might look like: daily math, Art Museum, hike with friends, use microscope. You probably already know what your child loves and does on their own and what has to be planned. I never set a goal of reading because my kid does that all the time anyway.

I encourage you to find some kind of co-op or local homeschooling group. Even if your kid doesn't need the support, you very well might! These people are old hands and can tell you all about the cool free things to do that you never heard of and might not be able to otherwise afford. I'm a member of a co-op that meets every other week in a church basement and periodically throughout the school year. The parents teach classes and the kids get to have the valuable experience of being taught by someone other than their parent. Good socialization for everyone. We all need friends, and this can be the place to make them.

As far as curriculum, there is so much out there. Lots of quality free stuff and lots of very expensive, beautifully bound curriculum as well. There might be a homeschool expo in the late summer in your area, and this is a place where you can go to look at all the vendors with their beautiful books. If you can afford to buy from them, great! I can't, so we buy used materials online. Amazon or eBay has this stuff. This is another reason to get in touch with your local co-op, because sometimes parents have a huge dump of all their materials when they are finished with them.

I recommend getting a school ID for yourself and your child. It sounds silly, but simply providing this card can get you into activities and experiences with grace. For some reason, my simply showing up and stating that I'm an educator is sometimes met with skepticism. I guess I'm just not believable? Anyway, here this link: https://www.homeschoolbuyersco-op.org/homeschool-id/

As far as structure, think about how your normal day is set up. We naturally get up early, so we will walk the dogs, work out at the Y, do school work and/or field trips in the morning, then my kid reads or plays in the afternoon. Unless it's a co-op day or a field trip is scheduled for the afternoon, and then we do that. Some families stay up really late and don't get going until 11 am. Some families spend 8 hours a day doing school work some days, then take off across the country for 2 week field trips. Some families don't do any school work at all. Those are the unschoolers. I don't have that much faith in my kid's ability to absorb what she needs to know without direct instruction, so that's not what we do.

Here are the resources I love at the moment: Map, Charts, & Graphs, Modern Curriculum Press workbooks (social studies); Greek & Latin Roots, Liane B. Onish (language arts); Vocabulary Ladders, Timothy Rasinski (language arts); Perplexors, Mindware (logic); https://www.postcrossing.com/ (geography/cursive); local library; state conservation department; microscope

Resources that look good , but I haven't tried: http://notebooksforstudents.org/homeschoollaptopdiscount.htm; http://www.eequalsmcq.com/?utm_source=E%3DMcQ+Holiday+Sale+2018&utm_campaign=LabNotes+Holiday+2018&utm_medium=email
